rv.q: Evans’ send-up of [Dickens’] classic… is so informed and quick-witted it doesn’t just fly the flag for intelligent parodies it salutes Dickens’ genius. English eccentricity at its madcap best.
It’s that kind of show, with nothing new to say about our Victorian past (far less the present), and lots of funny ways of saying it.
Yet despite Leslie’s boisterous direction, Evans’ satiric flair and a thoroughly entertaining ensemble, this is a long haul.

'Bleak Expectations' could let itself off the leash more. Still, Evans knows how to turn running gags into plot elements and vice versa — whatever that anvil prop cost, it was worth it...I just couldn’t help wishing it had come a good half-hour sooner.
The comedy here is familiar, thin stuff, both exhausted and exhausting.

Zany Dickensian-inspired mayhem has landed at Piccadilly Circus in the form of a period farce with more Charles Dickens references than you could feasibly shake an ebony silver-topped cane at — and there really couldn’t be a more fitting venue to host such a Victorian comedy melodrama, than The Criterion. Serena Manteghi, J.J.
But the show unwittingly perpetuates the prejudice it seeks to disparage.
There is lots to enjoy here; the constant silliness means there nothing serious in the show, but that is exactly the point.
The pace of Caroline Leslie’s production is hectic and the shouting sometimes excessive.
The performances lift a tired and shtick-filled script but likely by nowhere near enough to satisfy an audience paying West End seat prices for a show with a big celebrity name.
Even comic exaggeration wears out its welcome if it isn't anchored in some kind of truth.
Its inoffensive silliness is enough to put a smile on the face of all but the most demanding theatregoer.

cn.t: This Dickensian parody earns praise for its wit and enthusiastic performances, but critics find the comedy thin and exhausting across two hours, with most agreeing the concept works better on radio than stretched for the stage.
